title: Internal files add to evidence of an ExxonMobil climate deception campaign
gist: Previously undisclosed documents from Massachusetts's lawsuit against ExxonMobil show company scientists privately doubting the feasibility of its algae biofuel and carbon-capture claims while ads promoted them, alongside a 1988 memo and 1997 API strategy that map Exxon's climate playbook. The release coincides with Supreme Court arguments in Boulder's case that could decide whether two dozen other suits proceed.

insights.claim: Newly released filings in Massachusetts's 2019 lawsuit against ExxonMobil include previously unpublished internal documents, including the full 1988 Sprow memo and recent Exxon scientist statements challenging the company's biofuel and carbon-capture claims.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: New primary-source evidence strengthens the state's deception case and Exxon's litigation exposure.
insights.locator: Sprow's memo is part of a batch

insights.claim: The Massachusetts attorney general argues Exxon deceived consumers and investors into believing it was acting to limit warming when its efforts were largely public relations, and seeks fines and an injunction.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Unlike other suits, this one targets consumer/investor deception, a different liability path.
insights.locator: The case brought by the Massachusetts attorney general

insights.claim: Exxon denies misleading the public or investors and calls the lawsuits meritless attempts to usurp policymakers' role.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Exxon's stated defense frames the fight as a policy-versus-courts question.
insights.quote: We believe the legal and factual theories set forth in these proceedings are meritless
insights.locator: Exxon did not respond to requests for comment

insights.claim: The US Supreme Court heard arguments this week from Exxon and Suncor Energy seeking to halt Boulder, Colorado's lawsuit, a decision that could determine whether more than two dozen other claims against oil companies proceed.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: The ruling is a binary catalyst for the entire climate-liability docket against oil majors.
insights.locator: This week, the US Supreme Court

insights.claim: Public Citizen's Aaron Regunberg argues oil companies are fighting to block discovery because they fear the public seeing evidence of decades of knowing deception, and that the filings show only a sliver of it.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Advocates frame discovery, not merits, as the key risk for defendants.
insights.quote: How many more reports are they sitting on?
insights.locator: Aaron Regunberg, director of climate accountability

insights.claim: Climate-driven extreme weather costs have topped $100 billion in the US in four of the last five years, while Exxon reported nearly $19 billion in earnings in the first half of this year.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: The cost-versus-profit gap underpins plaintiffs' cost-recovery rationale.

insights.claim: An Exxon scientist testified that the company's 2018 press release promising 10,000 barrels per day of algae biofuel by 2025 was misleading, with 'all the clauses' patently false and the target completely impossible.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Sworn testimony that a flagship green claim was false is potent evidence of greenwashing.
insights.quote: All the clauses in there are patently false.

insights.claim: The scientist said he told others at Exxon the target was impossible before the press release was issued, and that a publicly touted algae breakthrough was actually a dead end.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Internal knowledge preceding public statements is central to proving deception.

insights.claim: Exxon later dropped algae biofuel research, after a public relations campaign that internal documents show scientists had told executives was infeasible, per a March Wall Street Journal report.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Marketing-led R&D claims can carry legal risk once abandoned.
insights.locator: In March, The Wall Street Journal reported

insights.claim: A 2014 Exxon presentation listed obstacles to commercial-scale carbon capture, including the need for 'massive investment', storage comparable to current oil and gas production, high costs and no market-based incentives.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Internal assessments of CCS economics contrast with public enthusiasm.
insights.locator: A 2014 presentation on Exxon's carbon capture portfolio

insights.claim: In 2017 an Exxon scientist said he was 'not a big fan' of calling the company a carbon capture leader, since its operations were mostly gas-processing plants whose technology 'has nothing to do' with capture for power plants and industrial facilities.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Leadership claims relied on a narrower technology than the one being promoted.

insights.claim: A 2017 presentation ranked algae and carbon capture ads among Exxon's highest performing, labelling them 'All-Around Winners', and a 2021 campaign aimed to make political and financial leaders 'believe ExxonMobil is committed to helping solve climate change'.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: The ads were evaluated as messaging assets, supporting the PR-over-action thesis.

insights.claim: Despite its scientists' doubts, Exxon continued promoting solutions unlikely to scale, while most of its money went to oil and gas, whose production it plans to expand more than 15 percent by 2030.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Capital allocation shows the low-carbon pitch is peripheral to the business.

insights.claim: Frank Sprow's November 1988 memo set Exxon's climate R&D goals as 'Protect the value of our resources' and 'Preserve Exxon's business options', and warned a worldwide consensus on action could cause substantial negative impacts on Exxon.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: The earliest strategy framed climate research as defense of reserve value.
insights.quote: Protect the value of our resources (oil, gas, coal)
insights.locator: Sprow then laid out an agenda

insights.claim: Sprow recommended embedding Exxon staff at leading modeling centers such as Princeton, monitoring nuclear, solar and biofuels, and seeking a research breakthrough that aligned with company business; he told the WSJ the memo was adopted as corporate policy.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Exxon deliberately kept scientific proximity and optionality on alternatives.
insights.locator: With modeling critical to climate science

insights.claim: A newly published memo of a 1997 API climate steering group meeting before Kyoto recommended continuing to 'question the scientific basis and cite the high economic cost' of climate policies, citing polling on what would resonate with the public.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Documents the coordinated industry messaging strategy ahead of the first major climate treaty.
insights.quote: continue to question the scientific basis and cite the high economic cost

insights.claim: Exxon planned to fund Jonathan Adler's CEI project but asked to narrow it to impacts on individuals and trade competitiveness, and API worked with the American Enterprise Institute to prevent misuse of an economists' letter by advocates of near-term action.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Think-tank funding was steered toward the cost-of-policy narrative.
insights.locator: It also said Exxon was planning to fund

insights.claim: Geoffrey Supran calls the 1997 memo 'the playbook all in one place', a sophisticated strategy to weaponize experts to perpetuate denial; Adler rejects that, saying CEI's work was accurate and consistent with its principles.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: The characterization of motives remains disputed between researchers and funded parties.
insights.quote: This is the playbook all in one place.

insights.claim: By 2005 Exxon said the scientific evidence 'remains inconclusive', yet by 2016 an Exxon scientist who contributed to the IPCC warned colleagues about climate tipping points, expected to become more probable with temperature change.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Public stance lagged internal scientific awareness for years, and later shifted as the Paris Agreement and shareholder concern grew.
insights.locator: By 2005, when Exxon was facing public criticism
